props.title: Van Helsing

sections.content: Van Helsing (2004) represents Universal Pictures' ambitious attempt to revive their classic monster properties in a single, action-packed blockbuster. Following Hugh Jackman's monster hunter through a CGI-heavy Victorian world, it draws direct inspiration from Universal's golden age of horror, particularly Dracula (1931) and Frankenstein (1931). Director Stephen Sommers applies the same high-energy approach that made The Mummy (1999) successful, but cranks up the supernatural elements to create a monster mash-up that's more focused on spectacle than scares.

sections.content: The early 2000s saw a trend of reimagining classic horror properties as big-budget action spectacles. While Van Helsing aimed to unite Universal's monster universe, Underworld (2003) created its own mythology mixing vampires and werewolves. Blade (1998) had earlier proven that horror characters could anchor action franchises. These films prioritized wire-work stunts, CGI creatures, and martial arts over traditional horror atmosphere. SUBHEAD: The Universal Monsters Legacy

Van Helsing's greatest strength lies in its loving references to Universal's classic monster films. The black-and-white prologue directly homages Frankenstein (1931) and The Wolf Man (1941). Richard Roxburgh's Dracula channels both Bela Lugosi's iconic performance and Gary Oldman's romantic take from Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992). While the action-heavy approach disappointed horror purists, the film celebrates Universal's monster legacy through production design, creature effects, and atmospheric Transylvanian settings.
